subject: Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water

messages.author: 12f62e4b4f2146dc
messages.subject: Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
parts:
Hi,

I've been setting up an INLA model to make some inferences on spatio-temporal tendencies of count data observed at different sites near the coast line in bays/inlets etc.

These counts are not observable on land so I need to specify a boundary for inla.mesh.2d so that my spatial random field only considers the body of water.

Is there an easy way to do this with mapdata (ie worldHires)?

I have polygons of land masses but am finding it hard to do this with bodies of water and each attempt with inla.nonconvex.hull() has produced really jagged meshes with far too many nodes at the boundary.

Another option could be to have multiple inner domains in my mesh separated by land (then I don't think having the outer domain overlap land would matter so much).

Is this possible with inla.mesh.2d?

Any advice or help would be greatly appreciated, thanks!

Hayden

I think I understand the process you have gone through with your code and have tried modifying it to my project.

Sorry to bug you further but I am having some issues using worldMapEnv {maps} with region: "New Zealand" as the land boundaries are missing a key island in my area of interest.

So I am trying to using nzMapEnv {maps} instead which has a nicer land boundary, but doesn't appear to be getting my islands as polygons (see below)

#================================================#
# nz_ocean_mesh.R

library(maps)
library(maptools)
require(INLA)

## NZ hi resolution map data
data(nzMapEnv)

## Define bounds on area of interest (top of south island NZ)
latBnd <- c(-41.40542, -40.56764)
longBnd <- c(172.6450, 174.4448)

## Create NZ map object
nz <- map("nz", fill = TRUE,
          col = "transparent",
          plot = FALSE)

## Create region index
(IDs <- sapply(strsplit(nz$names, " "), function(x) x[1]))
IDs <- c(1:length(IDs))

## Convert land boundaries to spatial polygons
nz.sp <- map2SpatialPolygons(
  nz, IDs = IDs,
  proj4string = CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84"))

## Area of interest (AoI)
box.sel <- matrix(c(longBnd[1],longBnd[2],longBnd[2],longBnd[1],
                    longBnd[1],latBnd[1],
                    latBnd[1],latBnd[2],latBnd[2],latBnd[1]), 
                  ncol = 2)

## Convert AoI to spatial polygon
sel.box <- SpatialPolygons(list(Polygons(list(Polygon(
  box.sel, FALSE)), '0')), proj4string = nz.sp@proj4string)

## Plot AoI with map
par(mar = c(3,2,1,1))
plot(sel.box)
plot(nz.sp, add = TRUE)
#================================================#

for (i in 1:length(nz.sp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons)) {
  pi <- nz.sp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[i]]
  coo.sel <- seq(1,nrow(pi@coords),5)
  text(pi@coords[coo.sel, 1], pi@coords[coo.sel, 2], paste(coo.sel))
  text(pi@labpt[1], pi@labpt[2], paste(i))
}

Everything looks good until this loop where my NZ spatial polygons object has only one polygon:
length(nz.sp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons) = 1

Whereas your equivalent has length 146:
length(ca.sp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons) = 146

Within my area of interest there are two islands I would like to define as holes as well as the main land mass (South Island of NZ)

Is this something to do with the proj4string string argument in nz.sp <- map2SpatialPolygons(...

Or a compatibility issue with nz <- map("nz", ... rather than nz <- map("world", "New Zealand", ...

I would be extremely grateful if you had any suggestions as to where I might be going wrong.

Also your paper "Applying Bayesian spatio-temporal models to fisheries bycatch in the Canadian Arctic" is really interesting!!
An amazing insight into the real world applications of INLA and SPDE's.

Thanks again,
Hayden

messages.author: 12f62e4b4f2146dc
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
parts:
Hi again,

Sorry for the long winded issue before, I think I may have solved my problem now,

Changing the indexing to the first @Polygon of the ith nz.sp@polygon seems to be doing the trick:

#================================================#
for (i in 1:length(IDs)) {
  pi <- nz.sp@polygons[[i]]@Polygons[[1]]

coo.sel <- seq(1,nrow(pi@coords),5)
  text(pi@coords[coo.sel, 1], pi@coords[coo.sel, 2], paste(coo.sel))
  text(pi@labpt[1], pi@labpt[2], paste(i))
}

#================================================#

Thanks,
Hayden

Just a tip: using different color the centroids plot make it easier to
identify the polygon you need, for example:

text(pi@labpt[1], pi@labpt[2], paste(i), col='red')

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
parts:
Consider that a SpatialPolygons object is a collection of *Polygons* and
that each one can have several *polygon* objects. In such code I took
the coordinates for the first *polygon* of the first *Polygons*, the
'coo1' object. Then I selected some coordinates of this set of
coordinates in order to build 'pl1'.

Elias

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Defining a inla.mesh.2d for a body of water
parts:
Hi Giulia,

The code I've posted is for the case where you have only one or a few
boundaries restrictions. For more it needs a different approach. Maybe
the Daniel's code at
http://www.r-inla.org/examples/case-studies/simpson2011 to make a mesh
over the oceans help you. If you need to define a model over the entire
Earth instead, you can use
mesh <- inla.mesh.create(globe=m)
where 'm' is the subdivision resolution, for example m=5 gives 252
nodes, m=10 gives 1002 nodes.

Elias
